newsitem.title: LATVIA: Stability the key for Baltic currencies.
newsitem.headline: Stability the key for Baltic currencies.

text.p: After quitting the former Soviet Union in 1991, the Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia launched their own currencies to get them out of the rouble zone as quickly as possible.
The aim of these currency reforms was to bring stability back to countries shaken by the end of Soviet central planning and help them on their way to market economies, analysts say.
LITHUANIA
The litas currency has been pegged to the dollar at four to one since 1994 under a currency board.
The currency board is a crude but effective way of creating stability and confidence in a currency by linking it directly to the country's foreign currency reserves at a fixed rate.
The currency board means a central bank cannot simply print money to finance the government as any rise in local currency in circulation has to be backed by a rise in foreign currency.

The Lithuanian authorities, amid assertions by some exporters that the currency board has led to an over-valued litas, wants to end the currency board and return to the central bank its traditional powers of monetary management.
The government and central bank says any change will be introduced in three stages, beginning with the re-introduction of money market management tools such as repurchase auctions.
The IMF says it would accept a change if it was done slowly and cautiously and in the right conditions.
ESTONIA
A currency board is also the anchor on which the Estonian kroon is pegged at eight to one German mark.
Here however there has been no pressure to end the system although again some exporters say the kroon is over-valued.
But most politicians, bankers and businessmen see the currency board as the bedrock of Estonia's economic performance, which has outstripped that of Latvia and Lithuania.
They say they would only change it if the kroon was going to be linked to the planned single European currency, the euro.
LATVIA

Latvia chose a slightly more flexible system than its Baltic neighbours. It operates a peg of the lat against the SDR at 0.7997 but without a currency board. The lat can fluctuate in a one percent range either side of this central rate.
The central bank has powers to intervene to buy or sell lats but tends to do this passively, with banks approaching it when the lat reaches either side of its one percent corridor.
The central bank's key rate is its refinancing rate but it also influences rates via repurchase rates and the rates at which banks can deposit lats at the central bank.

The lat has rarely suffered from speculative attacks except in 1995 when its largest bank, Banka Baltiya collapsed. Then, the lat fell as low as 0.70 to the dollar, versus a more usual 0.52/0.54, and the central bank was forced to intervene.
